title: Kulasekara and the Buddha Tooth
subtitle: The Five Brothers of Ma'abar and the Tooth of the Buddha
region: Madurai, Sri Lanka, Kayalpattinam and the Ma'abar coast
moral: Power is tested by what it returns as well as what it wins.

sources.citation: Marco Polo, The Travels, Book III, ch. XVI; Henry Yule ed. and trans., 3rd ed. (1903)
sources.note: Near-contemporary eyewitness account of Ma'abar, pearls and the five royal brothers.

sources.citation: Mahavamsa/Culavamsa, ch. 88; Wilhelm Geiger trans., Pali Text Society (1930)
sources.note: Primary Sri Lankan source for the Tooth Relic seizure and diplomatic return.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Pandyan Kingdom (1929); Noboru Karashima, A Concise History of South India (2014)
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of inscriptions, foreign accounts and chronology.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of Kulasekara on a sea cliff, ships behind him

dialogue.text: In Kulasekara’s age, five Pandyan brothers ruled pearl-bright Ma'abar—until one sailed to Sri Lanka, seized the Buddha’s Tooth, and then chose to send it back.

panels.shot: slow push-in from bustling port to Kulasekara in court

dialogue.text: Marco Polo saw Ma'abar’s shore in these years—crowded quays, pearl divers, horse traders—and heard of five royal brothers sharing the Pandyan crown from Madurai.

panels.shot: medium court shot, Kulasekara flanked by unseen brothers (silhouettes/background)

dialogue.text: In inscriptions and chronicles, Maravarman Kulasekara emerges as the leading brother, ruling roughly from 1268 to 1308, bound to his siblings by blood and by power.

panels.shot: wide shot of coastal trade, slightly elevated viewpoint

dialogue.text: The Ma'abar coast fed their strength: foreign horses landed here, pearls gleamed in baskets, customs dues flowed to Madurai. Wealth linked them to the Indian Ocean world.

panels.shot: intimate court interior, Kulasekara in discussion with a learned advisor (advisor not in cast)

dialogue.text: Across the narrow sea lay Sri Lanka, riven by rival kings. Pandyan influence occasionally touched the island; now, the chronicles say, Kulasekara turned his gaze there.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle of Kulasekara boarding a ship

dialogue.text: The Culavamsa, the Sri Lankan chronicle, tells of a Pandyan king named Kulasekara who gathered ships and men, and sailed to the island as an invader from the mainland.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of Pandyan fleet on the sea

dialogue.text: The Palk Strait lay between them and their goal. Wind filled their sails. Somewhere ahead stood Polonnaruwa and the most treasured object in Sri Lanka’s Buddhist world.

panels.shot: wide shot of Pandyan troops outside a Sri Lankan city

dialogue.text: The Culavamsa speaks with anguish of Pandyan forces entering the island, of cities threatened and rulers challenged. Behind its words lies the shock of foreign arms at the heart of the island.

panels.shot: solemn interior of a relic shrine, dramatic chiaroscuro

dialogue.text: At the center of the chronicle’s lament is one act: the Tooth Relic of the Buddha, kept in a jeweled casket, is said to have been seized by Kulasekara’s men and taken from the shrine.

panels.shot: close-up on Kulasekara holding the reliquary, face unreadable

dialogue.text: “This relic shall sail with us now,”
For the Sinhalese authors, the Tooth was not a mere treasure. It embodied kingship and the Buddha’s presence. Its loss was recorded as a disaster for the island.

panels.shot: wide shot of Pandyan fleet returning, shrine silhouette fading

dialogue.text: With the relic on board, the fleet turned back across the sea. The Culavamsa describes the Tooth Relic being carried away to the Pandyan land, leaving monks and kings to grieve.

panels.shot: regal interior in Madurai, relic casket set apart

dialogue.text: Yet the same chronicle also tells of negotiation. Lankan envoys petitioned the Pandyan court; letters and pleas crossed the sea, seeking the Tooth’s return from Kulasekara.

panels.shot: medium shot, Kulasekara in reflective pose by the casket

dialogue.text: The Culavamsa presents a turning: after talks and agreements, Kulasekara ordered the relic to be sent back. The same king who took it chose to relinquish it.

panels.shot: wide shot of a single ship bearing the relic towards Sri Lanka

dialogue.text: The chronicle describes the relic’s journey back, under Pandyan protection, to be restored to the island. For Sri Lanka’s Buddhists, it was a recovery of sanctity and legitimacy.

panels.shot: ceremonial interior in Sri Lanka, focus on monks and relic

dialogue.text: The Culavamsa frames the episode from the island’s side: foreign seizure, deep distress, diplomacy, and finally rejoicing as the Tooth Relic was again enshrined in its home.

panels.shot: split-focus composition: Madurai wealth on one side, distant memory of Sri Lanka on the other

dialogue.text: In South Indian histories, Kulasekara stands among strong Pandyan rulers, enriching Madurai and its coasts. In Sri Lankan memory, he appears as the mainland king who once took, and then restored, their holiest relic.

panels.shot: close-up on Kulasekara’s calm, weathered face, eyes looking past the viewer

dialogue.text: His age reminds us: power is measured not only by what it can seize from others, but also by what it chooses to give back when the world asks for its return.
